title: Problem Solving in the Mathematics Curriculum: From Domain-General Strategies to Domain-Specific Tactics https://bera-journals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/curj.213
author: Barton, Craig
source: Tips for Teachers (tipsforteachers.co.uk), December 18, 2024 — original paper:
summary: Barton summarizes Colin Foster's paper arguing against teaching general, domain-general problem-solving strategies (like 'be systematic' or 'draw a diagram') in favor of explicit instruction in specific, domain-specific tactics — for example, 'draw an auxiliary line' in geometry. Foster contends that concrete, actionable tactics are more teachable and more transferable to genuine non-routine problems than broad heuristics, and he lays out a sequence for teaching them: pick problems the tactic dramatically unlocks, let students struggle first without the tactic, then teach it explicitly, practice it across varied problems, and interleave it with other tactics so students learn to discriminate between them. The paper distinguishes routine from non-routine tasks and argues that thorough content teaching alone is not sufficient for developing problem-solving skill — tactics need to be taught on top of content knowledge, not assumed to emerge from it automatically.
points: Foster argues for teaching narrow, content-specific problem-solving tactics (e.g. 'draw an auxiliary line') rather than broad domain-general strategies like 'be systematic,' which he says are too vague to be actionable.

The recommended teaching sequence is: let students struggle with the problem first, then teach the tactic explicitly, then practice it across varied problems, then interleave it with other tactics to build discrimination.
Choosing problems that the target tactic 'dramatically unlocks' helps students appreciate the tactic's power rather than treating it as an arbitrary instruction.

Teaching content thoroughly is not, on its own, sufficient to build problem-solving skill — Foster argues tactics must be explicitly taught alongside content, not assumed to emerge from content mastery alone.
quotes: It argues against the use of general problem-solving strategies, proposing instead the explicit teaching of specific, content-related tactics.

Domain-specific tactics are more concrete and actionable, and students are more likely to be able to apply them successfully. Teaching broad domain-general strategies such as “be systematic” or “draw a diagram” is not helpful for students.

Teachers should allow students to struggle with problems initially, without explicitly teaching them the tactic. This will help students to develop their own problem-solving skills and to appreciate the value of the tactic when it is introduced.

Teachers should interleave problems that require different tactics. This will help students to learn to discriminate between different tactics and to choose the most appropriate tactic for a given problem.

Breaking down some of the highest leverage of Polya's strategies into detailed, actionable, domain-specific tactics, focused on well-defined content areas, seems to have the potential to mobilize students' potentially inert content knowledge in the service of powerful problem solving of non-routine problems.
Teachers should create a coherent problem-solving curriculum that systematically addresses important, high-leverage tactics.
